GUI usage
python run.py web

Open http://127.0.0.1:5000 (or the address set in Setup). A sidebar on the left carries the six pages — Fine-tune, Quantize, Deploy, Environment, Setup and Documentation — and, beneath them, the state of the GPU: which card is present, how much of it is free, and a warning in amber when another application is holding most of it. That line is in the sidebar rather than on a page because it applies to all of them.

Each page follows the same shape: an input panel at the top, then progress, then either the result or the error, only ever one of the three at a time. Errors appear in place, where the result would have been; the small notices in the top-right corner are for things that pass — a copy confirmed, a stage started. Every row of every result has a copy button at its right-hand end.

Fine-tune

The five steps are collapsible panels. The first is open; answering one collapses it, marks it done with its answer in the header, and opens the next. Any panel can be reopened by clicking its header, and changing an earlier answer un-answers the later ones — so a new model cannot leave a previous model's estimate behind.

1. Base model. Type to search: the suggestion list refreshes as you type, showing the top twenty by trending score, filtered to models whose name starts with what you typed. Models already on this machine carry a downloaded badge. Arrow keys move through the list and Enter takes the highlighted one; Enter with nothing highlighted takes exactly what you typed, so a full identifier can always be entered by hand. Tick Only models already downloaded for the local list instead.

2. Training dataset. Drop the JSON file onto the zone, or browse for it. It is validated on upload; if it cannot be used, every problem is listed in a table with its location, and the step stays open so the list remains in view.

3. Parameters. Each field carries its explanation underneath it. Booleans are switches. The bar above loads a stored preset and saves the current values as a new one.

4. Pre-flight estimate. Runs the same prediction as the terminal, and shows what it is made of: parameter count, vocabulary, peak memory required against memory available. When it does not fit, the shortfall and the remedies are listed too. The Run button stays disabled until it passes.

5. Run. Training and the merge that follows it report into a progress panel below the steps, with a live bar. When it finishes, the merged model's path is shown with a link to the Quantize page.

Quantize

Pick a merged model and an output type; the explanation of the selected type is shown beneath it. Types needing llama-quantize are absent from the list entirely when that binary is not installed. Model name is filled with the original model's name whenever you pick a model, and can be changed; the file it will produce is shown beneath it as you type. Left empty, the original name is used. The finished file is reported with its size, and its path can be copied.

Deploy

Pick a GGUF and a runner. Only installed runners appear. A name for Ollama is proposed from the file's model name and quantization, so a model renamed when it was quantized keeps that name; you can change it. When the deployment finishes, the command that runs the model is shown ready to copy.

Environment

The same report as python run.py check: the card and its memory as headline figures, then every operation, whether it is available, and the reason when it is not. Deployment targets are listed the same way.

Setup

Two panels set the two directories: Model directory for checkpoints, adapters and merged models, and Output model directory for quantized GGUF files. Each shows the default it falls back to. Type a path and press Save, or press Browse… to pick a folder: the browser opens inside that panel on the current directory, a click on a folder opens it, Up returns to its parent and the drive list switches drive. Use this folder saves the folder on screen. To use a folder that does not exist yet, browse to its parent, then type the new name at the end of the path and press Save. The directory is created if needed and must be writable, otherwise the reason is shown in place. Restore the default returns that panel to its default. Neither directory can be changed while a stage is running, since that stage would otherwise write its first artefacts in one place and its last in another.

The Web server panel sets the IP address and port python run.py web listens on, 127.0.0.1:5000 by default. The address must be an IP address of this machine: 127.0.0.1 keeps the interface on this computer, 0.0.0.0 listens on every network interface, and a specific address listens on that interface only. A warning is shown for any address other machines can reach — the server has no authentication, reads local files and starts processes. The change applies the next time the web server starts; the running server keeps its current address. Restore the default returns to 127.0.0.1:5000.

Documentation

This manual is available inside the interface — the chapters below are the ones it carries. The search box above them opens the chapters that match and marks every occurrence. The full PDF can be downloaded from the same page.

Why fine-tuning is normally out of reach

A language model is mostly a stack of weight matrices. Training updates every one of them, and each weight needs more than its own storage while that happens: the weight itself, its gradient, and the optimiser's running averages. With the Adam optimiser in mixed precision that comes to roughly sixteen bytes per parameter.

For a 7-billion-parameter model that is about 112 GB, before a single activation is stored. No consumer GPU comes close.

Two techniques, used together, bring it down to something a laptop can do. LoRA reduces what must be trained. Quantization reduces what must be held. The combination is QLoRA.

LoRA

LoRA — Low-Rank Adaptation — starts from an observation about what fine-tuning actually changes. Adapting a model to a new task does not scatter arbitrary changes across a weight matrix; the update has a strong internal structure. It has, in the usual phrasing, a low intrinsic rank.

If the update is low-rank, it does not need to be stored as a full matrix.

Take a weight matrix W of shape d_out × d_in. Instead of learning a full update ΔW of the same shape, LoRA learns two much smaller matrices:

    B  of shape  d_out × r
    A  of shape  r × d_in

where r, the rank, is small — typically 8 to 64 against dimensions in the thousands. Their product B @ A has the shape of ΔW, but is constrained to rank r. The layer computes:

    y = W x + (B @ A) x · (alpha / r)

W is frozen. Only A and B are trained.

The saving is dramatic. For a 4096 × 4096 matrix, a full update is about 16.8 million parameters. At rank 16, A and B together are 131,072 — 0.8%. In a whole model, LoRA typically trains well under 1% of the parameters, and the optimiser state shrinks in the same proportion.

The scaling factor

The update is multiplied by alpha / r. Because it is a ratio, raising the rank without raising alpha weakens the adapter: doubling r while alpha stays put halves the scale. The convention alpha = 2r keeps the effective scale at 2 whatever the rank, which is why the two are usually changed together.

Initialisation

A is initialised randomly and B to zeros, so B @ A is exactly zero at the start. The adapted model therefore begins as an exact copy of the base model, and training moves away from it smoothly. Initialising both randomly would inject noise into a working model before it had learned anything.

Which layers to adapt

In a transformer block, adapters are usually attached to seven projections:

  • Attention — q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj. These govern what the model attends to.
  • MLP — gate_proj, up_proj, down_proj. These are much larger and hold most of the model's factual capacity.

Adapting all seven gives the best quality. Attention-only is the cheapest useful subset, and a reasonable first thing to cut when memory is short.

QLoRA

LoRA shrinks what is trained. The frozen base model still has to be held — and at two bytes per parameter, a 7B model is 14 GB before training starts.

QLoRA quantizes those frozen weights to four bits, cutting them to about 3.5 GB. Three ideas make that work without wrecking the model.

NF4, the 4-bit NormalFloat. Neural network weights are approximately normally distributed around zero. An evenly spaced 4-bit grid would waste most of its sixteen levels out in the tails where almost no weights live. NF4 places its levels so that each holds roughly the same number of weights — information-theoretically optimal for normally distributed values, and markedly better than uniform 4-bit at the same size.

Double quantization. Weights are quantized in small blocks, each with its own scale factor. Those scale factors are themselves numbers taking space — enough to matter. Double quantization quantizes them too, saving around 0.4 bits per parameter for no measurable quality cost.

Computing in higher precision. The stored weights are 4-bit, but arithmetic is not. Each block is dequantized to bfloat16 as it is needed, used, and discarded. The memory saving is in storage; the mathematics stays accurate.

The gradient still flows through the frozen quantized weights to reach the adapters — the base model participates fully in the backward pass. It simply is never updated.

What it costs

Roughly, for a 7B model:

Table 1 — Memory for a 7B model: full fine-tuning against QLoRA

Full fine-tune QLoRA
Base weights 14 GB (bf16) 3.9 GB (4-bit)
Gradients 14 GB ~5 MB
Optimiser state 56 GB ~20 MB
Total, before activations ~84 GB ~4 GB

Quality is close. The original QLoRA work found 4-bit adapted models substantially matching 16-bit fine-tuning across a range of tasks. The base model is degraded slightly by quantization, and the adapters partly compensate by training against the quantized weights they will actually run alongside.

The term nobody expects

One tensor often dominates memory on small models: the logits. The output is batch × sequence × vocabulary, and modern vocabularies are large. At 2048 tokens with a 152,000-token vocabulary, that single tensor is around 600 MB in bfloat16 — and the loss computation needs a float32 copy and a gradient at the same time.

For a 0.6B model with 4-bit weights of under 400 MB, the logits are the largest single allocation in the run. This is why a small model can fail to fit when the arithmetic on its parameter count says it should, and why reducing the sequence length helps so much more than intuition suggests.

Merging

Training leaves you with two things: the untouched base model, and a small adapter. Inference could load both and add their outputs, but that means an extra matrix multiplication in every adapted layer, forever.

Merging removes it. Since the adapter's contribution is a plain addition:

    W_merged = W + (B @ A) · (alpha / r)

...it can be computed once and folded into the weight. The result is an ordinary model of exactly the base model's shape and size, indistinguishable in structure from any other. There is no adapter left, no inference overhead, and no runtime dependency on the adapter library.

It also makes the model convertible. GGUF conversion, and the tools that consume GGUF, understand ordinary models — not base-plus-adapter pairs.

Why it runs on the CPU, unquantized

Merging deliberately loads the base model at full precision, on the CPU.

The adapter was trained against 4-bit weights, but merging into 4-bit weights would be self-defeating: adding a small, precise update to a coarsely quantized value and re-quantizing the result would round most of the update away. The update has to land in weights precise enough to record it.

That makes merging a system-memory operation, not a VRAM one: about 2.5 bytes per parameter, roughly 19 GB for a 7B model. Output is written in shards so the whole model is never serialised at once.

The merge is exact. It is arithmetic, not approximation, and nothing is lost beyond bfloat16 rounding.

Quantization

The merged model is two bytes per parameter — 15 GB for a 7B. That is fine for a server and awkward for a laptop. Quantization trades a little quality for a lot of size.

This is a different operation from the 4-bit loading in QLoRA. That was a training-time technique for fitting a frozen model into VRAM. This produces a file, in the GGUF format, for inference engines built on llama.cpp — which is what Ollama and LM Studio run.

How it works

Weights are grouped into blocks. Each block is stored as small integers plus one or two scale factors that map those integers back to real values. A 4-bit block of 32 weights costs 32 nibbles plus its scales — around 4.5 bits per weight all in, against 16 for bfloat16.

K-quants refine this by recognising that not all weights matter equally. Attention weights and the embedding table are more sensitive to error than the bulk of the feed-forward layers, so a "4-bit" k-quant is not uniformly 4-bit: it spends 5 or 6 bits where precision pays and 4 or fewer where it does not. That is what the _S, _M and _L suffixes mean — small, medium and large variants of the same nominal width, differing in how generously they treat the sensitive tensors.

The two routes

Some types are produced in one step, directly from the merged model. The k-quants need two: the model is first converted to f16 GGUF, then re-quantized by a second tool. This application does both automatically, and keeps the intermediate f16 file — it is a valid output in its own right, and a later k-quant of the same model reuses it instead of converting again.

Choosing a type

Table 2 — GGUF output types

Type Two-pass Description
f32 no No quantization. Four bytes per weight; a reference baseline, rarely worth shipping.
f16 no Two bytes per weight, effectively lossless for inference. Also the staging format for k-quants.
bf16 no Two bytes per weight with the exponent range of float32. Preferred over F16 for models trained in bfloat16.
q8_0 no Roughly one byte per weight and near-indistinguishable from F16. The default: the best quality-to-size trade for most users.
tq1_0 no Extreme compression for ternary-trained models. Produces unusable output on ordinary models.
tq2_0 no As TQ1_0, slightly larger and more accurate. Only for models trained ternary.
q2_K yes Smallest usable k-quant. Noticeable quality loss; for when memory is the binding constraint.
q3_K_S yes Aggressive 3-bit packing with uniform block sizes.
q3_K_M yes 3-bit with more precision spent on attention weights. Better than Q3_K_S at a small size cost.
q3_K_L yes 3-bit with the highest-impact tensors kept larger. Approaches Q4_K_S quality.
q4_K_S yes Compact 4-bit k-quant. A good floor for quality-sensitive work.
q4_K_M yes The community default for local inference: about half the size of Q8_0 with modest quality loss.
q5_K_S yes 5-bit k-quant; quality close to Q8_0 at a meaningfully smaller size.
q5_K_M yes 5-bit with extra precision on sensitive tensors. Very close to lossless in practice.
q6_K yes Practically indistinguishable from Q8_0 while noticeably smaller.

For most purposes the useful range is narrow. q8_0 is the default here: about one byte per weight and effectively indistinguishable from the original. q4_K_M is the community's usual choice for local inference, roughly half that size with a modest quality cost. Below 4-bit, degradation becomes easy to notice, and is worth accepting only when memory is the binding constraint.

What it costs

Quantization error is not uniform. Perplexity — the standard aggregate measure — barely moves at 8-bit and rises gently through 5- and 4-bit k-quants. But aggregate scores hide where the damage lands: heavily quantized models tend to degrade first on the things that need precision, such as arithmetic, code, and long chains of reasoning, while ordinary prose still reads fine.

A fine-tuned model deserves a little extra care. If the behaviour you trained in is subtle, verify it survives at the quantization you ship, rather than assuming that a small perplexity change means a small behavioural one.

Training parameters

These are the values from LoraConfig and SFTConfig that the interface exposes. The table below is generated from the application's own parameter definitions, so it cannot drift from what the program actually accepts.

LoRA

Table 3 — LoRA adapter parameters

Parameter Default Accepts What it does
r 32 1 to 256 Width of the low-rank update. Each targeted layer learns two small matrices of this rank instead of a full weight matrix, which is what makes training cheap. Higher values add capacity, trainable parameters and VRAM roughly linearly. 8-16 suits small, narrow datasets; 32-64 suits broader ones.
lora_alpha 64 1 to 512 Scaling applied to the adapter output: the update is multiplied by alpha / r. Because it is a ratio, raising the rank without raising alpha weakens the adapter. The common convention is alpha = 2 x r, giving a scale of 2.
lora_dropout 0.05 0 to 1 Dropout applied to the adapter input during training only. Acts as regularisation against memorising a small dataset. 0.05-0.1 is usual; 0 is reasonable for large datasets or very short runs.
target_modules q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj, gate_proj, up_proj, down_proj q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj, gate_proj, up_proj, down_proj Which projection layers receive an adapter. The attention projections (q, k, v, o) change how the model attends; the MLP projections (gate, up, down) hold most of its factual capacity. Targeting all seven gives the best quality and costs the most memory; attention-only is the cheapest useful subset.
bias none none, all, lora_only Which bias terms are trainable. 'none' keeps the adapter smallest and is almost always correct; 'lora_only' trains biases on adapted layers; 'all' trains every bias and prevents a clean merge back into the base.

Which matter most. Sequence length and rank dominate memory. Rank and the choice of target modules dominate quality. Epochs dominate whether the model learns the material or memorises it.

A note on bias. Only "none" merges cleanly. "all" trains bias terms that have no place to be folded into a weight matrix, so a model trained that way cannot be merged into a plain model.

Supervised fine-tuning

Table 4 — Supervised fine-tuning parameters

Parameter Default Accepts What it does
num_train_epochs 15 1 to 1000 How many times the trainer walks the whole dataset. Small instruction sets need many passes to take effect; large ones overfit quickly. If answers start being reproduced verbatim, reduce this first.
per_device_train_batch_size 1 1 to 64 Examples processed together in one forward and backward pass. This is the single largest driver of VRAM use. Leave at 1 on consumer GPUs and raise the accumulation steps instead.
gradient_accumulation_steps 2 1 to 256 Number of batches accumulated before weights are updated. The effective batch size is this multiplied by the batch size per device, so it buys the stability of a larger batch at almost no extra VRAM cost.
learning_rate 0.0005 1e-06 to 0.01 Step size for the optimiser. LoRA tolerates rates one to two orders of magnitude above full fine-tuning because only the adapters move. 1e-4 to 5e-4 is the usual band; lower it if the loss oscillates.
warmup_steps 5 0 to 10000 Steps spent ramping the learning rate up from zero, which avoids a destructive first update on freshly initialised adapters. A handful is enough for short runs.
max_length 2048 128 to 131072 Token budget per training example; longer conversations are truncated. Memory grows with this value, so it is the most effective dial to turn when a run runs out of VRAM. Set it just above your longest example.
bf16 True true / false Run the forward and backward passes in bfloat16. Halves activation memory against float32 and, unlike float16, needs no loss scaling. Requires an Ampere or newer GPU.
gradient_checkpointing True true / false Discard intermediate activations and recompute them during the backward pass. Cuts activation memory substantially at roughly 20-30% slower training. Usually the difference between fitting and not fitting.

Effective batch size is the per-device batch size multiplied by the accumulation steps. Accumulation buys the stability of a larger batch at almost no memory cost, which is why the batch size stays at 1 on consumer GPUs and the accumulation steps go up instead.

Learning rate. LoRA tolerates rates one to two orders of magnitude above full fine-tuning, because only the small adapter matrices move. 1e-4 to 5e-4 is the usual band. If the loss oscillates rather than descending, lower it.

Epochs. The default of 15 suits a small instruction set of a few dozen examples, where a handful of passes would leave no trace. For thousands of examples it is far too many: if the model starts reproducing training answers verbatim, this is the first thing to reduce.

Gradient checkpointing discards intermediate activations and recomputes them during the backward pass — substantially less memory for roughly 20–30% slower training. On a consumer GPU it is usually the difference between fitting and not.

Quantization parameters

The output type is the only choice. Types marked as requiring llama-quantize are produced by the two-pass route and are unavailable when that binary is not installed.

Table 5 — GGUF output types and the tool each one needs

Type Two-pass Description
f32 no No quantization. Four bytes per weight; a reference baseline, rarely worth shipping.
f16 no Two bytes per weight, effectively lossless for inference. Also the staging format for k-quants.
bf16 no Two bytes per weight with the exponent range of float32. Preferred over F16 for models trained in bfloat16.
q8_0 no Roughly one byte per weight and near-indistinguishable from F16. The default: the best quality-to-size trade for most users.
tq1_0 no Extreme compression for ternary-trained models. Produces unusable output on ordinary models.
tq2_0 no As TQ1_0, slightly larger and more accurate. Only for models trained ternary.
q2_K yes Smallest usable k-quant. Noticeable quality loss; for when memory is the binding constraint.
q3_K_S yes Aggressive 3-bit packing with uniform block sizes.
q3_K_M yes 3-bit with more precision spent on attention weights. Better than Q3_K_S at a small size cost.
q3_K_L yes 3-bit with the highest-impact tensors kept larger. Approaches Q4_K_S quality.
q4_K_S yes Compact 4-bit k-quant. A good floor for quality-sensitive work.
q4_K_M yes The community default for local inference: about half the size of Q8_0 with modest quality loss.
q5_K_S yes 5-bit k-quant; quality close to Q8_0 at a meaningfully smaller size.
q5_K_M yes 5-bit with extra precision on sensitive tensors. Very close to lossless in practice.
q6_K yes Practically indistinguishable from Q8_0 while noticeably smaller.

The quantization block size and the per-tensor precision assignments are llama.cpp's own and are not exposed: they are properties of each named type rather than independent settings.
